page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E6.Ax.Flex.16-256 is an x86_64 virtual instance configured with an elevated memory-to-vCPU ratio. The virtual machine executes on AMD EPYC 9J45 processors operating at a base frequency of 2.7 GHz. Compute resources consist of 16 dedicated physical cores with multithreading enabled, delivering 32 vCPUs. System memory is provisioned at 256 GB, resulting in an allocation of 8 GB per vCPU.

Hardware specifications indicate no integrated hardware accelerators, as the GPU count is zero. Additionally, the instance provides no onboard local storage, necessitating external network-attached block volumes for filesystem persistence and data storage. Network configuration includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. Dedicated CPU allocation ensures computing cycles remain isolated from neighboring virtual machines.

With an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, the hardware configuration targets workloads where RAM capacity is the primary constraint. This hardware balance reduces the need to over-provision compute cores merely to obtain sufficient memory capacity. Workload fit includes in-memory databases, distributed memory caching frameworks, large-scale ETL pipelines, and enterprise application runtimes requiring substantial heap allocations.
description: The Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E6.Ax.Flex.16-256 is a memory-oriented virtual compute instance built on the x86_64 architecture. Powered by an AMD EPYC 9J45 processor running at 2.7 GHz, the server provides 16 dedicated physical cores yielding 32 vCPUs via multithreading. It is equipped with 256 GB of system RAM, offering an allocation of 8 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include integrated GPUs or local solid-state storage, requiring remote cloud storage volumes for file persistence. One complimentary public IPv4 address is provisioned by default. The dedicated CPU mapping prevents resource contention, delivering predictable compute execution across concurrent threads. Given its high memory density relative to core count, this configuration is technically aligned with workloads requiring substantial memory footprints, including in-memory databases, large-scale enterprise data caching, memory-intensive batch processing, ETL workflows, and data analytics pipelines.
